turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels, process/composition
    columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B, Al, Cu, W, S, Heat
    treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment
    step 1 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment
    step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3
    temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3 cooling
    rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1
    time, Secondary treatment step 2 temperature, Secondary treatment step 2
    time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4
    time, Thermal exposure temperature, Thermal exposure time) and the two
    measured objectives `yield strength (MPa)` and `elongation (%)` (both at
    room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose objectives were
    NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same process/composition
    columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH elongation (%). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), elongation (%)) plane, so a set of
mutually non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates
that are all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
I would select a **frontier-spanning set**, using close composition/process matches in the training data rather than ranking candidates by strength alone.

| Candidate | Intended role | Training-data support |
|---|---|---|
| **c018** | High-elongation endpoint | Its composition and primary heat treatment match a training steel with **278 MPa yield strength and 62% elongation**. Its additional thermal exposure makes those values an analogue, not a direct prediction. |
| **c051** | Ductility-rich intermediate | A nearly identical steel, solution-treated at 1150°C rather than 1100°C, achieved **375 MPa and 53%**—an attractive improvement in strength while retaining substantial elongation. |
| **c078** | Middle of the trade-off | The same composition treated at 1085°C rather than 1065°C achieved **520 MPa and 37%**. This is strong local evidence for a useful middle-frontier candidate. |
| **c074** | Higher-strength intermediate | Its Ni–Ti-rich composition matches training steels whose aging routes produced **590–1000 MPa with 25–29% elongation**. Its two-stage aging makes it a plausible bridge toward higher strength, although this pick carries more process-related uncertainty. |
| **c053** | High-strength endpoint | A closely related composition with the same 450°C tempering temperature achieved **1380 MPa and 15% elongation**. This offers better frontier potential than many candidates associated with roughly 700–1000 MPa and similar elongation. |

These picks target complementary regions of the expected frontier. In particular, they avoid spending several slots on the numerous moderate-elongation tempered steels that may add little hypervolume once a strong endpoint is included. The cited properties are **measured training analogues**, not measured pool outcomes.

Final: c018, c051, c078, c074, c053
